newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy and France seek to patch up EMU row.
newsitem.headline: Italy and France seek to patch up EMU row.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, who incensed Italy by saying it could be left out at the launch of a European single currency, patched things up with Rome in time for a summit this week, political sources said.

The sources told Reuters Chirac called Prime Minister Romano Prodi by telephone late on Tuesday after the Italian leader failed to get through to him earlier in the day to demand an explanation for the French president's remarks.
A furious Prodi had been about to scrap a summit in Naples on Thursday and Friday until Chirac mended his gaffe.
"The conversation was cordial," one of the sources said.

Prodi's centre-left government, stung by the second diplomatic row in as many days as it prepares to present its punishing 1997 "Budget for Europe" to parliament, launched a vocal campaign to try to convince its partners it was on track.

"We intend to be among the founders of the EMU (Economic and Monetary Union) in 1999," Treasury and Budget Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Washington.

"We can face the future in Europe in the role of co-protagonist," Prodi told reporters in Rome, where he pointedly toasted the opening of new offices for his centre-left Olive Tree coalition with Italian champagne.
"Italy is a country that, when it is on the ropes, always has the capacity for rebirth," he said.

Chirac, speaking during a visit to the depressed textile town of Arras, said those countries which had made an effort to clean up public finances would speed towards the magic date of January 1, 1999, when the euro, the EU currency, is due to be launched.
"It may take a little bit longer for those who are further behind, like Italy," Chirac said.
After frantic diplomatic activity, a warning from deputy prime minister Walter Veltroni not to meddle in Italian affairs and threats from Rome to call the October 3-4 summit off, Chirac rowed back.

Some analysts believe his remarks had been a bid to bolster France's hand in talks on the level of the lira's return to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism. It crashed out amid currency chaos in 1992 and Prodi wants it to go back as soon as possible.
"I believe the Italian government is fully determined to do everything, as it has shown in its budget, to be in the first wave of countries to join the euro," Chirac said.
"Of course, I ardently hope it will succeed."

Prodi was forced into a drastic re-think of his budget sums after discovering that Spain was not interested in trying jointly to renegotiate the tough economic targets required to qualify for monetary union in order to gain more time.
Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said in an interview on Monday that Madrid had no intention of "holding hands" with Italy and would be in EMU right from the start.
Before the summit begins on Thursday, Prodi's government is due to present the controversial deficit-busting budget to the lower house of parliament, where the opposition is lining up.

"The remarks made by the French president and Spanish prime minister have blown apart in less than 48 hours the lies of the Prodi government," Silvio Berlusconi, leader of the main opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance, said in a statement.

The package aims to cut a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit with the help of a one-off "Euro-tax". Opposition and business leaders have slammed Prodi for failing to cut pensions and healthcare provisions.
"There's no plot by France or Spain against Italy -- there's irritation...in the face of Prodi's attempts to get into Europe without paying the bill," far-right leader Gianfranco Fini said.
But Italian state auditor Andrea Monorchio insisted Italy would hit a key three percent ratio of deficit to gross domestic product required for EMU entry.
"The budget is sufficient to get Italy into the single currency," he told state radio.
